qualitative.3m: RNAi platform pioneer with proprietary GalNAc-siRNA delivery conjugates and dominant global patent estate across rare genetic diseases (hATTR, AHP, PH1) and cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM). Commercial pricing power is extraordinary ($300k-$500k/patient/yr) with gross margins >85%. FY2025 HELIOS-B expansion validated platform economics as revenues surged 81% to $3.71B and GAAP net income turned positive to $313.7M. Moat erosion threats include patent cliffs in the 2030s (~2035) and competing oral/gene-editing modalities.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced to 5Y by fatal-flaw substitution threat (4_sub=2) from one-time curative in vivo CRISPR gene editing (NTLA-2001) alongside moderate pressure from entrants (4_ent=1), rivalry (4_riv=1), and buyer pushback (4_buy=1).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). While Alnylam's RNAi platform achieved commercial profitability in FY2025 following the landmark HELIOS-B ATTR-CM expansion, biotechnology has an empirical base-rate persistence of only 10-15 years (Tier 3). Crucially, the franchise faces an active terminal disruption headwind from one-time curative in vivo CRISPR gene editing (Intellia/Regeneron NTLA-2001 Phase 3 MAGNITUDE trial) which permanently eliminates hepatic TTR production, threatening to render chronic lifelong quarterly RNAi injections obsolete. Compounding patent expirations in ~2035 and oral small-molecule competition (BridgeBio Attruby) cap CAP at 5 years (< 15 hurdle).
qualitative.evidence: Over 2016-2024, Alnylam posted continuous GAAP net losses (peaking at -$1,131M in FY2022 and -$278M in FY2024) with negative 5-year median GAAP ROIC (-65.9% to -100%) due to massive clinical development expenses. In FY2025, commercial uptake of Amvuttra (vutrisiran) following the HELIOS-B Phase 3 trial and FDA approval for ATTR-CM drove an 81% surge in net product revenue to $2.99B and total revenue to $3.71B, delivering its first annual GAAP net income of $313.7M and operating profit (EBIT) of $501.6M. Cash stood at $1,657.2M against ~$1.0B in convertible debt. Extreme orphan drug pricing power ($300k-$500k/patient/year) yields gross margins >85%. However, structural biotechnology runway is tightly constrained: primary composition of matter patents expire around 2035, oral competitors like BridgeBio's acoramidis are expanding, and one-time in vivo CRISPR gene editing therapies (NTLA-2001) threaten to permanently displace chronic quarterly RNAi maintenance therapy.

qualitative.3m: Patented FcRn antagonist platform (Vyvgart / efgartigimod) enjoys high clinical switching costs and neurologist brand equity in generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG) and CIDP. High orphan pricing ($225k+/year) and rapid commercial adoption generated >$4B in 2025 product sales, swinging GAAP ROIC to >25%. However, long-term persistence faces direct competing FcRn biologics (J&J nipocalimab, UCB rozanolixizumab) and finite patent runway.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced to 5Y by fatal-flaw competitive rivalry (4_riv=2) from mega-pharma FcRn rivals (J&J nipocalimab, UCB Rystiggo) alongside fast-clock-speed substitution and patent cliff risks (4_sub=1), entrants (4_ent=1), and buyer pricing pressure (4_buy=1).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Single-product commercial biotech relying almost entirely on Vyvgart (>95% of revenues). Under the Mauboussin persistence framework, biotech is Tier 3 (10-15Y baseline), and faces sharp haircuts due to near-term FcRn competition from mega-pharma rivals (J&J nipocalimab, UCB Rystiggo) and primary patent expirations in the early 2030s, capping the Competitive Advantage Period at 5 years (well below the 15-year threshold).
qualitative.evidence: While Vyvgart commercial sales scaled rapidly to $2.2B in 2024 and $4.2B in 2025 generating $1.29B in net profit, argenx's 5-year median GAAP ROIC is -6.1% due to clinical-stage cash burn before 2024. More crucially, revenue is overwhelmingly concentrated in a single molecule whose primary composition-of-matter patents expire around 2031-2033. Aggressive competing FcRn entrants (J&J, UCB, Immunovant) and bio-similar threats prevent confidence in a 15+ year durable competitive advantage period.

qualitative.3m: Pioneering antibody discovery platform (DuoBody, HexaBody), but Genmab acts primarily as a royalty taker on J&J's Darzalex without independent pricing power, facing an imminent 2029 US patent cliff.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Genmab is an antibody engineering pioneer but operates primarily as a contractual royalty recipient on J&J's Darzalex (accounting for 65-80%+ of revenue). It possesses zero independent pricing power to increase royalty rates above inflation and faces a major unhedged 2029 US patent cliff after losing legal arbitration on Darzalex Faspro.
qualitative.evidence: Genmab's high historical GAAP ROIC (>20%) is heavily distorted by passive royalties on Johnson & Johnson's Darzalex sales. Genmab has no discretion over realized drug pricing, which faces mandatory Medicare IRA price negotiations in the US and statutory cuts in Europe. With core Darzalex US patents expiring in 2029 and EU in 2031, Genmab faces severe revenue and margin compression, forcing costly defensive pipeline M&A (e.g., ProfoundBio for $1.8B) that expands invested capital while high-margin royalty streams evaporate.

qualitative.3m: Rare disease portfolio (hematology/immunology) built largely via debt-fueled in-licensing and acquisitions rather than proprietary discovery, resulting in bloated intangibles and severe product write-downs.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Sobi lacks an enduring organic R&D moat, relying on debt- and equity-fueled acquisitions to mask structural patent expirations in core hemophilia assets. Capital allocation missteps—epitomized by the SEK 17.1B acquisition of CTI BioPharma followed by a massive SEK 6.6B impairment on Vonjo in 2025—depress multi-cycle GAAP ROIC well below the 12% hurdle.
qualitative.evidence: Sobi's rare disease commercialization model has suffered heavy capital misallocation: the acquisition of CTI BioPharma underperformed commercially, forcing a SEK 6,612M pre-tax write-down in 2025 that crushed operating profit to SEK 867M and net income to SEK 478M. On an invested capital base bloated by goodwill and intangible rights (>SEK 35B), GAAP ROIC fell to low single digits in 2025, pulling 5-year median GAAP ROIC below the 12% requirement. Flagship hemophilia drugs (Elocta, Alprolix) face ongoing technological substitution.

qualitative.3m: Oligopolistic distribution scale alongside McKesson and Cencora, handling ~25% of US pharmaceutical volume. However, CAH is a pure pass-through logistics intermediary with razor-thin operating margins (~1.0%) and zero unconstrained pricing power over either upstream branded drug manufacturers (who set WAC prices) or consolidated downstream PBMs/health systems. Demonstrated by the 2024 loss of the OptumRx contract (16% of sales, ~$33B) during competitive RFP rebidding. Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC is sub-hurdle and severely impaired by $6B+ in opioid litigation liabilities, with persistent negative book equity (-$2.9B in FY2025).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). Thin-margin (~1% operating margin) wholesale drug distributor operating as a pass-through intermediary between pharma manufacturers and consolidated PBMs/retailers. Possesses zero unconstrained pricing power; demonstrated by customer churn when OptumRx (16% of sales) defected to McKesson in 2024. Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC is severely impaired by $6B+ opioid litigation liabilities and negative book equity (-$2.9B in FY2025), failing the Munger capital-efficiency standard.
qualitative.evidence: CAH operates in a tight oligopoly alongside McKesson and Cencora (controlling 90%+ of US prescription drug distribution) with FY2025 revenue of $254.2B, but operating margins remain microscopic at 1.03% ($2,613M EBIT) and gross margins are ~3.2%. Upstream branded drug prices are fixed by manufacturers, while downstream PBMs and retail pharmacy chains exert severe pricing pressure; in FY2024, CAH lost its contract with OptumRx (~$33B / 16% of revenue) to McKesson during renewal bidding. Historical GAAP ROIC has been deeply negative in crisis years (FY2019: -46.8%, FY2021: -31.4%) driven by $6B+ in opioid litigation liabilities, and book equity remains negative (-$2,883M in FY2025) with negative tangible equity of -$16.5B against $7.0B in long-term debt. Even with OptiFreight logistics and specialty distribution growth, CAH is structurally a low-margin commodity logistics provider lacking pricing power >= inflation.

qualitative.3m: Rational 90%+ US drug distribution oligopoly protected by irreplaceable physical cold-chain logistics, regulatory licenses, and deep workflow integration with health systems and community oncology. Fee-for-service contracts and specialty distribution protect real gross profit, sustaining multi-cycle GAAP ROIC well above 50%.

Entrants (4_ent=0), suppliers (4_sup=0), and substitution (4_sub=0) remain structurally benign given unreplicable physical cold-chain logistics.
qualitative.note: Passes all 6 gates. Indispensable US pharmaceutical distribution oligopolist handling ~one-third of domestic prescription volume with leading oncology and specialty franchises. Formidable moat rooted in physical cold-chain logistics, deep provider integration, and high switching costs. Resilient across all 5 macrotrends with demographic aging as a durable volume tailwind. Exceptional FCF conversion (>150%) and conservative net debt (<2.1x net income). [5-10Y g: rx/specialty volume 4.5% + specialty mix/acquisitions 1.5% - wholesale contract repricing drag 0.5% + share repurchases 2.5%]
qualitative.evidence: FY2025 revenue reached $321.3B with EBIT of $2.63B and Owner FCF of $3.06B, delivering FCF conversion of 167.5% of net income. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 97.0% (operating ROIC >100%) due to rapid working capital turns and fee-for-service / specialty contracts. Oligopolistic market structure (>90% controlled by Cencora, McKesson, and Cardinal Health) prevents price wars. High-margin specialty leadership reinforced by Retina Consultants of America ($4.4B cash outlay) and OneOncology integration. Balance sheet carries $4.36B cash against $7.54B debt, yielding net debt of $3.19B (~1.0x Owner FCF), with the core Walgreens prime vendor agreement secured through 2029.

qualitative.3m: Henry Schein benefits from switching costs in its proprietary practice management software (Dentrix, Dentrix Ascend) and significant scale in dental/medical distribution logistics. However, its economic moat has been structurally eroded by rapid consolidation of dental practices into corporate Dental Support Organizations (DSOs) wielding intense pricing leverage, alongside transparent online e-commerce competition and peer rivalry (Patterson, Benco). Operating margins have collapsed from ~7.2% in FY2019 to ~4.95% in FY2025. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 9.78%, well below the 12% hurdle, with FY2023-FY2025 hovering at 8.9%-9.8% even after full cyber incident normalization, proving lack of real pricing power.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 9.78% < 12%, lack of pricing power >= inflation, REJECT). While Henry Schein maintains established scale in dental distribution and practice software (Dentrix), structural consolidation of solo dentists into corporate Dental Support Organizations (DSOs) has shifted purchasing leverage upstream, compressing GAAP operating margins from ~7.2% (2019) to ~4.95% (2025). The sub-10% GAAP ROIC persists beyond the temporary late-2023 cyberattack, driven by $4B+ of debt-funded M&A that diluted capital returns ($5.2B goodwill/intangibles vs. $3.2B equity, $2.3B debt). Peak-to-peak Owner EPS has stagnated below 2019/2021 levels ($4.68 in FY2025 vs. $5.38 in FY2019), failing the Munger moat and pricing power standard.
qualitative.evidence: Multi-cycle financial track record demonstrates structural capital efficiency erosion: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 9.78%, failing the 12% threshold (FY2021: 17.14%, FY2022: 13.43%, FY2023: 9.78%, FY2024: 8.86%, FY2025: 9.50%). Operating margins compressed from 7.19% in FY2019 and 6.87% in FY2021 to 4.98% in FY2023, 4.90% in FY2024, and 4.95% in FY2025 on $13.18B revenue. Although the October 2023 BlackCat cyberattack caused operational disruption, operations normalized in 2024-2025 with $20M insurance recovery in Q1 2025, yet normalized ROIC remains under 10%. Balance sheet has deteriorated from serial M&A: LT debt expanded from $822M in 2021 to $2,310M in FY2025 (LT debt / Net Income of 5.8x; interest expense rose from $27M to $150M, lowering interest coverage to 4.35x), with $5,231M in goodwill and intangibles on $3,245M equity. Peak owner EPS has failed to compound ($4.68 in FY2025 vs. $5.38 in FY2019). Activist pressure from Ananym Capital and a $250M white-knight injection from KKR underscore ongoing structural governance and margin challenges under DSO buyer concentration.

qualitative.3m: Co-leads the indispensable 90%+ US pharmaceutical distribution oligopoly (~33% share) alongside Cencora and Cardinal Health, augmented by The US Oncology Network (2,600+ providers). Operating model functions as a vital toll booth with fee-for-service contracts and proprietary workflow integration (iKnowMed EHR) creating high switching costs. Empirical proof: Operating ROIC sustainably >50-100% on negative operating working capital, EBIT doubled from $2.49B (FY19) to $6.21B (FY25), and operating margins expanded despite massive throughput. Primary erosion threats: Regulatory scrutiny over oncology practice consolidation, PBM contract disputes, and biosimilar margin compression.

Threat of new entrants (4_ent=0), supplier pressure (4_sup=0), and substitution (4_sub=0) are structurally benign given indispensable physical cold-chain infrastructure.

Insulated from AI disruption and demographic aging acts as a powerful secular volume tailwind. Exemplary capital allocation under CEO Brian Tyler: pruned lower-margin European operations, settled opioid litigation, and retired ~50% of outstanding shares since FY16. Outstanding cash conversion (FCF/NI >130% 5Y average) and pristine balance sheet with 25x interest coverage and net debt of just 0.54x net income; negative book equity is purely an artifact of FCF-funded share buybacks and non-cash litigation charges. [5-10Y g: US pharma/specialty volume 4.0% + oncology/biopharma mix 2.0% + manufacturer fee price 1.0% - regulatory/biosimilar margin drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 3.0%]
qualitative.evidence: FY16-FY25 revenue expanded from $198.5B to $403.4B with FY25 EBIT reaching $6.21B and Net Income of $4.76B. Exceptional cash generation with FY25 Owner FCF of $5.47B (FCF conversion 115% in FY25, 5Y average >130%) on minimal capex requirements ($436M, ~0.1% of sales). Diluted share count reduced from ~230M in FY16 to ~116M in FY25, propelling Owner EPS from $25.00 (FY16 peak) and $8.04 (FY19) to $40.73 in FY25 (10Y CAGR 10.3%, 5Y CAGR >25%). Balance sheet is exceptionally robust with $3.98B cash against $6.53B total debt, yielding net debt of $2.55B (0.54x Net Income) and EBIT/interest coverage of 25.1x ($6.21B EBIT vs $247M interest expense). Nationwide opioid settlement is fully accrued with structured payout obligations easily absorbed by annual operating cash flows exceeding $6B.

qualitative.3m: Dominant Swiss pharmacy network and wholesale distribution infrastructure (Galexis/Alloga), but sub-hurdle 10% ROIC and triennial statutory FOPH/BAG drug price cuts prevent raising prices above inflation.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Dominant Swiss pharmacy network and healthcare distributor with resilient volumes, but 5-year median ROIC of 10.0% falls strictly below the 12% hurdle. Furthermore, triennial statutory drug price cuts and regulated dispensing margins mandated by the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH/BAG) permanently cap pricing power below inflation.
qualitative.evidence: Galenica generates consistent but structurally sub-hurdle returns on capital across 2021-2025: reported ROIC has ranged tightly between 9.2% and 10.1% (5-year median 10.0%, failing the >=12% test). Core prescription medicine revenue is subject to statutory price reviews by the Swiss FOPH (BAG) that enforce structural price cuts across reimbursable medicines, limiting top-line pricing power despite retail service expansion and generic substitution buffers.

qualitative.3m: Abbott's economic moat rests on high customer switching barriers and consumable toll-booth dynamics across Medical Devices and Diagnostics. FreeStyle Libre commands >50% global CGM patient volume with >8 million active users purchasing recurring bi-weekly sensor replacements at >70% gross margins. In Diagnostics, closed-loop Alinity/Architect analyzers lock hospital laboratories into proprietary multi-year reagent consumable contracts. Structural heart franchises (MitraClip, TriClip, Navitor) benefit from extensive clinician procedural training and high switching costs. Empirical proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 12.8%, tangible operating ROIC >25-50%, gross margins consistently 55-57%, and FCF conversion of 80.6%. Primary erosion risks include competitive encroachment from Dexcom in CGM, GLP-1 therapy penetration moderating intensive diabetes therapies, and preterm infant formula product liability claims.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced by -10Y for competitive rivalry in continuous glucose monitoring and diagnostics (4_riv=1), hospital GPO buyer bargaining power (4_buy=1), and medtech technology clock-speed substitution risk (4_sub=1). Entrants (4_ent=0) and suppliers (4_sup=0) remain benign.
qualitative.note: Passes all 6 gates. Global diversified medtech and healthcare leader anchored by the FreeStyle Libre CGM franchise, structural heart devices, closed-loop diagnostic lab analyzers, and leading pediatric/adult nutrition brands. Highly insulated from AI disruption and a prime secular beneficiary of global demographic aging. Fortress balance sheet with net debt of just $1.4B (0.2x net income) and 16.3x interest coverage; $670M NEC infant formula settlement is comfortably absorbed by normal cash flow. [5-10Y g: FreeStyle Libre & medtech device volume 5.5% + diagnostic & nutrition pricing 1.5% + emerging markets pharma mix 1.0% - margin/litigation drag 0.5% + share repurchases 0.5%]
qualitative.evidence: Abbott generates >$44B in diversified revenue across Medical Devices ($17B+, led by $7.6B Libre CGM and structural heart), Diagnostics ($9B+ core lab/point-of-care), Nutrition ($8B+ Similac/Ensure), and Established Pharmaceuticals ($5B+ branded generics). Capital efficiency is verified by a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 12.8% and tangible operating ROIC of 53.3%. Free cash flow conversion averages 80.6% ($6.7B FCF in FY2025 on $6.5B Net Income). De-leveraging discipline is exemplary: debt reduced from $27.2B post-St. Jude in 2017 to $9.9B in FY2025, offset by $8.5B in cash (net debt $1.4B vs. $8.1B EBIT; interest coverage 16.3x). 52 consecutive years of dividend increases (Dividend King). Post-COVID testing normalization is complete, with organic core device and diagnostic volumes resuming high-single-digit peak-to-peak earnings expansion.

qualitative.3m: Infusion pump installed bases (Spectrum, Novum IQ) provide modest switching costs via proprietary tubing sets and drug libraries, but the moat is structurally weak. Large-volume IV solutions, basic hospital consumables, and generic injectables are commoditized price-taker categories sold under multi-year fixed-price GPO contracts (Vizient, Premier). 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~6.5%, well below the 12% hurdle. Massive value destruction from the $12.4B debt-financed Hillrom acquisition ($3B+ goodwill impairment) and persistent FDA recalls confirm lack of pricing power and moat erosion against Becton Dickinson and ICU Medical.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & No Pricing Power, REJECT). 10-year median GAAP ROIC of ~6.5% falls far short of the 12% hurdle. Infusion pump switching costs are overwhelmed by commoditized IV solutions and hospital consumables sold under fixed-price GPO contracts that lack inflation pass-through power. Value-destructive capital allocation in the $12.4B debt-funded Hillrom acquisition and subsequent $3B+ impairment cement sub-hurdle returns.
qualitative.evidence: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is 6.5%. ROIC collapsed across 2020-2025 (2020: 9.0%, 2021: 3.5%, 2022: -8.5%, 2023: 2.3%, 2024: ~0.0%, 2025: -1.4%) driven by persistent margin compression from plastic/resin/freight inflation, FDA infusion pump recalls (Spectrum/Novum IQ), and a $3.1B goodwill impairment on Hillrom. Management acquired Hillrom in late 2021 for $12.4B enterprise value funded with >$11B of debt at cyclical peak, triggering severe leverage that forced the divestiture of its Kidney Care unit (Vantive) to Carlyle in January 2025 for $3.8B ($3.3B net cash) to pay down debt. Fragile supply chain highlighted by Hurricane Helene flooding its Marion, NC plant in late 2024, halting 60% of US IV fluid production.

qualitative.3m: BDX possesses extensive manufacturing scale in high-volume clinical consumables (syringes, needles, vacutainers, IV catheters) and installed infusion pump hardware. However, it fails proof of moat: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 5.45% (10-year range 2.0%-7.7%), well below the 12% hurdle. Dilutive mega-acquisitions (CareFusion $12.2B, C.R. Bard $24B, and Edwards Lifesciences Critical Care $4.2B) loaded the balance sheet with $36.0B in goodwill and intangibles on $25.4B of equity (negative tangible equity of -$10.6B). Pricing power is heavily constrained by hospital Group Purchasing Organizations (GPOs like Vizient, Premier) running competitive tenders on commoditized consumables. Moreover, chronic Alaris pump quality issues (2020-2023 FDA shipping hold, 2025 legacy bezel recall, 2026 Class I infusion set recall) have triggered pricing concessions and customer friction.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 5.45%, REJECT). Serial debt-funded mega-acquisitions (CareFusion, Bard, Edwards Critical Care) permanently burdened the capital base with $36B of goodwill and intangibles, suppressing GAAP ROIC to 2.0%-5.6% for eight consecutive years. Hospital GPO tender procurement caps pricing power on basic consumables, while multi-year Alaris infusion system Class I recalls erode commercial contracting leverage.
qualitative.evidence: 10-year financial history demonstrates chronic sub-hurdle returns on capital: GAAP ROIC was 7.71% in 2016, 7.06% in 2017, 4.24% in 2018, 3.59% in 2019, 2.02% in 2020, 5.56% in 2021, 5.46% in 2022, 5.03% in 2023, 5.02% in 2024, and 5.45% in 2025 (5-year median 5.45%, never exceeding 6% post-2017). As of FY2025, Goodwill and Intangibles stand at $36,001M against Total Equity of $25,390M, resulting in negative tangible equity of -$10,611M. Long-term debt of $17,621M represents 10.5x net income ($1,678M), exacerbated by $3.2B of new debt taken in 2024 to fund the $4.2B Edwards Lifesciences Critical Care acquisition. While FCF conversion is healthy (133% in FY2025) and operating cash flow reached $3,430M, the capital-diluted balance sheet and hospital GPO tender resistance prevent compounding at attractive economic rates.

qualitative.3m: High physician switching barriers and clinical procedural lock-in across catheter labs and operating rooms. Interventional cardiologists and electrophysiologists train extensively on Boston Scientific's proprietary hardware consoles and delivery platforms (Farapulse PFA generator, Watchman TruSpeed/FLX Pro LAAC delivery systems, SpyGlass DS direct visualization endoscopy). Once integrated into hospital workflows, treatment protocols, and inventory supply chains, switching to alternative platforms incurs severe capital re-equipment hurdles, clinical retraining, and staff re-credentialing. Proof of moat is reflected in 28.2% 5-year median operating (tangible) ROIC (reaching 42.1% in FY2025) and stable ~70% gross margins. Primary erosion threats stem from fast-follower PFA launches by Medtronic (PulseSelect/Affera), Abbott (Volt), and J&J (Varipulse), as well as clinical shifts in concomitant procedure scheduling.

qualitative.note: Passes all 6 gates. Global cardiovascular and interventional medtech leader anchored by Farapulse PFA, Watchman LAAC, and single-use endoscopy. Procedural switching costs and clinical training create durable lock-in, driving ~70% gross margins and >28% operating ROIC. Structural beneficiary of demographic aging with resilient 113% FCF conversion and 10.4x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: procedure volume growth 5.5% + premium innovation mix/price 1.5% + Axonics/tuck-in expansion 1.0% - PFA competition/pricing drag 0.5% + operating leverage/buybacks 0.5%]
qualitative.evidence: Multi-cycle track record of durable growth and operating leverage: Net sales expanded from $9,076M in FY2016 to $20,074M in FY2025 (~9.2% CAGR), with FY2025 organic growth reaching ~15.8% powered by Farapulse PFA scaling to over $1B in its first commercial year. GAAP EBIT expanded from $447M in 2016 to $3,613M in 2025, lifting operating margins from ~5% to 18.0% GAAP and operating (tangible) ROIC to 42.1% in FY2025 (5-year median 28.2%). Gross margins remain consistently defended at ~70.5%. Cash generation is exceptional, with Owner FCF conversion averaging well above 100% of GAAP Net Income (FY2025 Owner FCF of $3,359M on $2,892M NI = 116%; TTM conversion 113.2%). Balance sheet remains sound: Net debt of $9.17B against TTM NI of $2.89B equates to 3.17 years of earnings (<= 4.0x threshold), and EBIT/Interest coverage is 10.35x ($3,613M / $349M). S&P affirms A- investment grade rating. Tuck-in capital allocation demonstrated by successful Axonics integration ($3.7B, closed Nov 2024) in sacral neuromodulation. Normalization of growth to 5-6% in 2026 reflects competitive PFA entrants (MDT, ABT) and transient operational disruption from a late-August 2026 cyber incident, but the core procedural lock-in remains structurally intact.

qualitative.3m: Proprietary enzymatic sensor chemistry, micro-filament wire technology, FDA iCGM clearance, and tight automated insulin delivery (AID) pump integration (Tandem, Insulet) provide a defensible technological barrier. However, the moat is severely undermined by head-to-head competition with Abbott Laboratories (FreeStyle Libre), persistent 5-8%/year per-patient net ASP deflation from PBM retail pharmacy rebate concessions, and margin dilution from lower-priced over-the-counter lines (Stelo).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). Single-product continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) specialist operates in an intense duopoly against Abbott Laboratories (FreeStyle Libre). Dexcom lacks pricing power >= inflation: realized revenue per patient faces persistent structural annual ASP deflation driven by retail pharmacy channel rebate concessions, aggressive Abbott price competition, and lower-priced OTC expansion (Stelo). Volume growth cannot mask the structural absence of pricing power required by Munger's standard.
qualitative.evidence: Revenue grew from $1.93B in FY2020 to $4.03B in FY2024 and $4.66B in FY2025 driven by unit volume expansion, but GAAP gross margins compressed from ~68% in 2021 to 60.1% in 2025 due to manufacturing transition costs and pharmacy channel mix shift. Realized per-patient revenue has fallen from >$3,500/yr in legacy DME channels to <$2,000/yr in retail pharmacy and ~$1,000/yr for Stelo OTC. In Q2 2024, unexpected rebate concessions to secure pharmacy formulary placement and DME market share losses forced a major full-year guidance cut, triggering a >40% stock plunge. Dexcom cannot raise prices at or above inflation without immediately hemorrhaging market share to Abbott Libre.

Primary threat is Medtronic/Boston Scientific competition in mature TAVR and hospital DRG reimbursement pressure.

Divestiture of Critical Care to BDX for $4.2B cash sharpened pure-play focus on structural heart. Insulated from macro disruptions with massive demographic aging tailwind. qualitative.evidence: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 19.8% and tangible operating ROIC of 27.1%. FY2025 net sales reached $6.07B (+11.5% YoY) with gross margins sustained at 78-79%.
